claim: Bright/high-contrast surface details (indicator lights, saturated accents) pull the viewer's eye strongly and should be placed deliberately and sparingly to guide attention around the model -- and once one bright accent exists, a matching second one is often needed elsewhere specifically to balance it and pull the eye back, rather than leaving a single dominant bright spot.
supporting_evidence: Direct quotes (~26:50 and surrounding): "look how much attention pulls this light in here right which means we do need another lighting here to balance it okay so probably what i'm going to do is drop another light here... the whole purpose of this light [array] is to bring your eyes back to the model"
rejected_alternative: Leaving a single bright accent detail unbalanced by anything else
reason: An unbalanced single bright accent was observed to pull disproportionate visual attention; a second, corresponding bright element was added specifically to redirect the eye back into the composition.

claim: Secondary/tertiary surface details (decals, panel lines, small mechanical elements) generally read better when their material is dialed down to blend with the surrounding surface (darkened to match, or decal opacity/alpha reduced, e.g. to ~0.2) rather than left at full brightness/contrast -- the detail should be perceptible on close inspection without visually competing with the primary shape-defining features.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~51:31): "there's a detail here you can barely see it but it breaks the surface and that's the key right the key is not to shout the key's to just whisper okay so remember that"; demonstrated repeatedly by darkening decal colors and lowering decal alpha (e.g. to 0.2) after placing them.
rejected_alternative: Leaving every added surface detail at full brightness/contrast
reason: Full-brightness secondary details compete with primary shape-defining highlights for visual attention; dimming them keeps them present without overpowering the read of the overall form.

claim: Mirroring a set of decals/small objects placed via a radial or regular array intermittently fails silently (objects don't appear on the mirrored side, or appear misaligned) when the source object's origin isn't set to its own geometry -- this is the same origin-state gate already observed to break Symmetrize and the Mirror modifier on ordinary mesh objects, now confirmed on decal objects too. Fix: Shift+S > Origin to Geometry on the affected object, then retry the mirror.
supporting_evidence: Direct quote (~16:40, one of several recurring instances in this video): "let's grab this go to to front view let's see this origin point shift s into geometry ah okay let's apply the mirror so operations multiply shift s to geometry now it should work simply mirror wasn't deployed"
